newsitem.title: POLAND: INTERVIEW - Polish privatisation not a race - minister.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Polish privatisation not a race - minister.

text.p: The head of Poland's new Treasury Ministry, Miroslaw Pietrewicz, said on Thursday that he would implement the government's 1997 privatisation plan but the speed and the number of sell-offs was not his top concern.

The powerful new portfolio was created on October 1 under a reform of central government, taking over the privatisation ministry as well as the oversight of state assets from several other ministries.

"The treasury minister took over the tasks of the privatisation minister and we have a government (privatisation) programme which sets out the direction, pace and areas (of privatisation)...so what we will be doing, will be mainly a continuation," Pietrewicz told Reuters in an interview.

The government aims to sell 115 companies directly to investors and float at least five firms on the Warsaw bourse next year, including flotation of the giant KGHM Polska Miedz copper concern and a partial sell-off of Bank Handlowy SA.

Also planned for 1997 is a partial privatisation of the national air carrier LOT as well as the start of the process at telecommunications monopolist TPSA, several oil refineries and the energy sector.

Pietrewicz said however his ministry had a broader mandate than just selling state firms and would treat privatisation not as a goal but as a means of meeting the ultimate target of managing and disposing of state assets in the most efficient way.

"We are not going to act as if it was a race in terms of the timing and the number of privatised companies, because privatisation and reforms are not at risk...so we don't have to prove to anyone that we want a market economy in Poland," he said.

The centrist opposition charges that the ruling coalition, of the ex-communist social democrats (SLD) and Pietrewicz's Polish Peasant Party (PSL), has slowed privatisation and left large areas of industry untouched by reforms.
Some analysts feared a further slow-down after Pietrewicz, some of whose Peasant party colleagues have often been critical of privatisation, replaced the SLD's Wieslaw Kaczmarek.
Since Pietrewicz took over there have been no major privatisation deals -- but he told Reuters this merely reflected the fact that several had been clinched just before the changeover.

"In the final weeks of the privatisation ministry there was a pressure to close all pending projects so now we have some breathing space," Pietrewicz said. "There is no question of stalling necessary ownership changes," he added.

As privatisation minister, Kaczmarek broadly implemented policies worked out by Solidarity-rooted governments after the 1989 fall of communism, while the scholarly, grey-bearded Pietrewicz's views on privatisation were not widely known.

Kaczmarek, known for his tough bargaining and insistence on seeking the best terms for each individual deal, has stayed on in the new ministry as first deputy minister directly overseeing sell-offs and restructuring of state firms.

Pietrewicz said his ministry would soon start assessing the current case-by-case privatisation approach focusing on individual companies or sectors, before deciding whether any changes were necessary.

"This process (of selling off step by step individual companies or sectors) has to be reviewed from the viewpoint of economic effectiveness...perhaps it will require some adjustments or perhaps only small fine-tuning," he said.
"But I stress there is no question of blocking privatisation," Pietrewicz added.
He said the new ministry needed better yardsticks to measure the macroeconomic impact of privatisation decisions.
"I hope that in a year's time we will have certain tools allowing more efficient monitoring of (privatisation) processes," Pietrewicz added.
